newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's new president calls for quick election.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's new president calls for quick election.

text.p: Bulgaria's new president Petar Stoyanov was sworn in on Sunday and gave his support to opposition demands for a general election as soon as possible to break the country's political deadlock.
"Bulgaria wants elections as soon as possible, Bulgaria must get these elections," he told parliament.

The governing Socialists have offered elections by the end of the year but the opposition wants them sooner and has staged 13 consecutive days of mass protests against economic hardship and the Socialists' insistence on forming a new cabinet.
Stoyanov and his vice-president, Todor Kavaldzhiev, were sworn in by parliamentary speaker Blagovest Sendov.
Parliament was cordoned off by police but small crowds gathered behind the barricades as bells rang out from the adjacent Alexander Nevsky cathedral.
The ceremony was broadcast on national television and freezing temperatures kept many people at home.

Anti-government protesters, angered by 300 percent inflation that has reduced millions of Bulgarians to paupers, besieged and ransacked parliament last weekend in clashes with riot police in which 196 people were injured.

"We have to make the right choice, which is the European type of civilisation, to show our will and to build the conditions for our integration into the European Union and NATO," Stoyanov said in his inaugural speech.
The government has dragged its feet on European and NATO integration, anxious not to alienate its old allies in Moscow.
"The Bulgaria of the future should resemble the countries to which our children emigrate," Stoyanov said.
"We must offer our children the society in which they dream of living, here in Bulgaria." Many young, well-educated Bulgarians leave to seek a better life in wealthier countries.

Stoyanov has said he is prepared to grant the ruling Socialists the mandate to form a new cabinet denied them by his predecessor, Zhelyu Zhelev. The opposition vehemently opposes a new mandate and wants immediate elections.
Zhelev told Bulgarian television: "There is no sense in handing a formal mandate which will explode social peace."
The government of former communists, mired in a deep economic crisis blamed by opponents on its own ineptitude and corruption, scored a mere eight percent support in one opinion poll last week.
Socialist reformers said a quick election could solve the crisis, but hardliners were more cautious.

Party leader Georgi Parvanov said Stoyanov's call was "not sufficiently well argued" while reformist Filip Bokov told Reuters: "It is quite realistic to hold elections at the end of March if negotiated."
Ivan Kostov, leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), was jubilant. "This is a celebration for Bulgaria. Elections now!" he said.
The UDF invited supporters to a celebration concert near the parliament later on Sunday instead of to its usual anti-government rally.
The strain of 13 days of mass demonstrations and strikes showed when members of the Socialists' reformist wing and a small liberal Marxist party on Saturday founded a rival leftist coalition.
New Left in Bulgaria said it wanted economic reform of the kind introduced in most of ex-communist eastern Europe but which has barely begun in Bulgaria.
The Socialist divisions fuelled speculation that the party could lose its parliamentary majority, won in 1994 elections, even if granted a new mandate by Stoyanov.
Diplomats say a delay in elections could aid the Socialists as the polls would be held after a new agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which might quickly bear fruit.

The IMF has said it will complete talks on introducing a tight monetary regime, its condition for handing over financial aid, with a new government as soon as it is formed. Stoyanov pledged to seek agreement on urgent economic measures.
